purpose: Second blind test set for the Ahava AI triage / diagnostic assistant and ML early-warning engine. No case or diagnosis repeats set 1 (AHV-DX-01 to 20). Feed ONLY the `input` block (stage 1 items first). Score against `answerKey`, which must never be sent to the engine.

provenance.rule: Every diagnosis, vital sign, lab value and image comes from a peer-reviewed, open-access case report on PubMed Central. Nothing clinical is invented.
provenance.constructedFields: `patientNarrative` and `clinicianNote` are written for this test in plain words from the published facts; they are not the patient's or author's own words. A value of null means the source did not report it - do not fill it in.
provenance.images: Images are the figures in the source article. Download them from the PMC link. To simulate a phone upload, photograph the figure on a screen with a phone.
provenance.licence: All sources are open access. Check the licence on each article page before redistributing images outside internal testing.
provenance.contamination: All sources were published between August 2025 and October 2026.

complexityScale: straightforward = classic presentation, a competent junior doctor gets it; moderate = one misleading feature or needs a specific question asked; hard = the original clinicians got it wrong at first.
triageScale: SATS acuity: 1 = Red/emergency, 2 = Orange/very urgent, 3 = Yellow/urgent, 4 = Green/routine. `minimumAcceptableLevel` is the least urgent level that is still safe (numerically higher = under-triage). Where `acceptableLevels` is given, a level outside that range on the urgent side is over-triage.
stagingRule: Items with `withholdUntilStage` and the `stages` text are released only after the engine has given its answer for the previous stage. Score each stage separately where `stageLevels` is given.

input.patientNarrative: I'm home alone. About an hour ago I got a sudden, really bad pain in my right testicle, 9 out of 10, and I feel like I'm going to be sick. The same thing happened a few weeks ago but it went away on its own, so maybe I should just wait?
input.clinicianNote: 15M, previously well. Sudden severe right hemiscrotal pain, onset ~2 h before arrival, with nausea. Similar self-limiting episode some weeks ago. Exam: right testis high-riding with transverse lie, exquisitely tender, scrotal erythema, absent cremasteric reflex.

labs.name: Scrotal Doppler ultrasound
labs.value: absent intratesticular arterial flow on the right

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Right testicular torsion (540 degrees), testis viable
mustDetect: Sudden testicular pain in an adolescent = torsion until proven otherwise; surgery within 6 hours
A previous self-resolving episode (intermittent torsion) is a red flag, not reassurance
Must NOT advise waiting at home; do not delay surgery for imaging if the scan is not immediately available
answerKey.pitfall: The patient asks whether he can wait. Tests whether the engine resists the patient's own framing.
answerKey.outcome: Scrotal exploration within the window, detorsion, bilateral three-point orchidopexy; testis salvaged.

input.patientNarrative: Yesterday I had acupuncture on my upper back and shoulders for gym pain. Straight away my chest got tight, it hurt to breathe in and I was short of breath. I thought it would settle overnight but it hasn't. I smoke one or two cigarettes a day.
input.clinicianNote: 30M, BMI 22.8, light smoker, no history. Acupuncture to both trapezius and infrascapular regions yesterday; immediate pleuritic chest pain, tightness and dyspnoea; presented next morning. Tachycardic. Haemodynamically stable, oxygenating satisfactorily on room air. Reduced air entry and hyperresonance over left hemithorax; right side normal.

vitals.notes: Saturation 'satisfactory on room air' (value not reported); no hypotension

images.shows: Large left pneumothorax with near-complete lung collapse and subtle mediastinal shift
Left lung re-expanding; small right apical pneumothorax now visible

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Iatrogenic (acupuncture) left pneumothorax with evolving tension physiology, plus a smaller right apical pneumothorax (bilateral)
mustDetect: Chest pain and dyspnoea immediately after needling over the thorax = pneumothorax
HR 130 with mediastinal shift = evolving tension: needs a chest drain now
Bilateral needling means look at both sides
answerKey.pitfall: Normal oxygen saturation in a young man can falsely reassure a vitals-based model. The contralateral pneumothorax was only seen after the first was drained.
answerKey.outcome: Left 20 Fr chest drain with immediate relief; small right pneumothorax managed conservatively; full resolution.

input.patientNarrative: I have chest pain. I used to smoke but I've stopped. I'm healthy and don't take any medicines. I don't have heart problems in my family that I know of.
input.clinicianNote: 45F, ex-smoker, no cardiovascular history, no medication. Chest pain. 12-lead ECG: ST elevation V2-V4. Thyroid function was normal on a check 3 months ago.

labs.name: Coronary angiography + IVUS
labs.value: long smooth tapering of mid-to-distal LAD; IVUS shows intramural haematoma (true lumen compressed)

labs.name: Echocardiogram
labs.value: EF 52%, apical akinesia, sessile apical thrombus

images.shows: Diffuse LAD tapering; crescent-shaped intramural haematoma

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Anterior STEMI caused by spontaneous coronary artery dissection (type 2, intramural haematoma of the LAD) with newly diagnosed Graves' thyrotoxicosis and an apical LV thrombus
acceptableAlternatives: Anterior STEMI (full credit for triage; SCAD should be in the differential for a woman under 50 with few risk factors)
mustDetect: ST elevation = STEMI pathway now
In a woman under 50 without risk factors, think SCAD (conservative management usually preferred over stenting)
answerKey.pitfall: Triage is easy. The diagnostic test is whether the engine considers SCAD and checks thyroid function rather than assuming plaque rupture.
answerKey.outcome: Conservative management (aspirin, beta-blocker), methimazole, warfarin for the thrombus; LV function preserved at 3 months.

source.citation: Speziali N et al. J Clin Med 2026;15(13):4930

input.patientNarrative: (Mother) My 11-month-old has had an itchy rash for two months. It started on her tummy and now it's all over, with little pus spots on her hands and the soles of her feet. Two hospitals said eczema and gave creams, but it's getting worse. She scratches all night and nobody in the house is sleeping. She has no fever, no cough, no diarrhoea.
input.clinicianNote: 11/12 F. 2/12 generalized pruritic erythematous papules and papulovesicles, worst on palms and soles with superimposed pustules. Failed desonide and pimecrolimus. Severe nocturnal itch, irritability. Systemically well, stable vitals. Crusted papules in finger webs and over MCP joints; excoriations on trunk.

labs.name: Household history (on direct questioning)
labs.value: parents and maternal grandparents all developed persistent itch ~7 weeks ago; mother (a ward nurse) has itchy papules in finger webs and armpits and nursed a patient with scabies 9 weeks ago

labs.name: Dermoscopy of sole lesion
labs.value: burrow with dark triangular structure at the end ('jet with contrail' sign)

images.shows: Papulovesicles and pustules on both soles; crusted papules in finger webs

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Infantile scabies (misdiagnosed as refractory eczema), acquired from household contacts
mustDetect: Itchy palm/sole pustules in an infant + finger-web lesions + no response to steroid = scabies
Ask whether other household members itch
Treat the whole household at the same time
answerKey.pitfall: Over-triage test: a well infant with a skin rash is routine. Diagnostic test: the engine must ask about household itch rather than accept 'eczema'.
answerKey.outcome: Sulfur ointment for infant, whole family treated, linen boiled; clear at 2 weeks.

source.citation: Guo Q et al. Front Med 2026;13:1919356

input.patientNarrative: I'm here for my hernia operation. I feel fine, honestly. I just got back from a game-hunting trip in Africa - that's where the old hernia repair gave way when I was lifting an animal. The nurse says my temperature is very high.
input.clinicianNote: 52M, pre-operative holding area for elective left inguinal hernia repair. Recently returned from a hunting trip in sub-Saharan Africa. Asymptomatic. Routine pre-op observations: temperature 41.1 C (106 F). Two black eschars - one on the back, one on the right shin.

images.shows: Black necrotic eschars on the back and right shin

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: African tick bite fever (Rickettsia africae), probable - clinical diagnosis from eschars, fever and travel
keyDifferentials: Falciparum malaria (must be excluded in any returning traveller with fever)
mustDetect: Fever 41.1 C - cancel elective surgery
Fever after Africa: malaria test is mandatory
Eschar + fever after bush exposure = tick-borne rickettsiosis: start doxycycline
answerKey.pitfall: An asymptomatic, cheerful patient with a single extreme vital sign. Tests whether the engine weights the measured temperature over the patient's 'I feel fine'.
answerKey.outcome: Surgery cancelled; 10 days of doxycycline; afebrile at 2 weeks and hernia repaired uneventfully.

input.patientNarrative: For four days I've had headache, dizziness, fever, vomiting, tummy pain and sore joints. I took paracetamol, ibuprofen and papaverine but it didn't help. My period is about two months late. I had Ebola last year and recovered, so they brought me to the Ebola unit.
input.clinicianNote: F 30s, G3P1, amenorrhoea 8+2 weeks. 4/7 fever, headache, dizziness, vomiting, abdominal pain, arthralgia. Ebola survivor (13 months ago); admitted to an Ebola treatment unit as suspected relapse. Alert, not pale or jaundiced. Abdomen soft, mild pelvic pain. Cervix posterior, long, closed. Uterus slightly enlarged; small left adnexal mass palpable; slight pain on cervical motion. CRT < 3 s. No ultrasound available in the unit.

stages.2: 10 hours after admission: increasing pelvic pain worst on the left, nausea, small vaginal bleed with clots, tachycardic and tachypnoeic, SpO2 96%, CRT ~4 s, Hb 10 g/dL, platelets 265,000.
stages.3: 19 hours after admission: sudden sharp stabbing left pelvic pain then bright red vaginal bleeding; restless, hypotensive, tachycardic, abdomen distending with generalized tenderness, painful pouch of Douglas, pale, cool peripheries, CRT > 6 s, Hb 8 then 6 g/dL.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Ruptured left tubal (ampullary) ectopic pregnancy with haemorrhagic shock, with concurrent falciparum malaria
mustDetect: Positive pregnancy test + pelvic pain + adnexal mass = ectopic until proven otherwise, even when malaria is also positive
Stage 2 (tachycardia, bleeding, falling Hb) = act before shock
Needs ultrasound / surgical capability - arrange transfer early
answerKey.pitfall: A positive malaria test and the Ebola context explained the fever, so the ectopic was labelled 'threatened abortion' until the patient was in shock.
answerKey.outcome: Laparotomy at 30 h: 3 L haemoperitoneum, left salpingectomy, 3.45 L blood transfused; survived and later had a normal pregnancy.

source.citation: Imani-Musimwa P et al. Front Med 2026;13:1848720

input.patientNarrative: (Parent) Our son is five and a half. Two weeks ago his gums at the top started swelling. Then he started limping on his left leg, and now he can't walk at all and cries when you move his legs. His gums bleed by themselves. The X-rays were normal and they said it was hip inflammation and gave anti-inflammatories, but he's worse. A biopsy of his jaw showed only inflammation. He has speech delay.
input.clinicianNote: 5.5M, consanguineous parents, language delay (speech therapy since 4), growth persistently < -2 SD, vaccinated. 2/52 painless maxillary gingival hypertrophy; MRI: 2.4 cm left maxillary lesion; biopsy non-specific inflammation. 1/52 progressive left limp; hip X-ray and ultrasound normal; treated as transient synovitis with NSAIDs. Now unable to stand. Pale, T 37.2. MUAC 12 cm. Severe pain on passive leg movement, knee flexion contractures, long-bone tenderness, power 4/5 limited by pain. Spongy bleeding gums, poor dentition, left facial swelling, petechiae on legs, conjunctival pallor. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

labs.name: ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement; HIV, hepatitis, CMV, EBV, parvovirus serology
Diet history (on direct questioning)
labs.value: since age 2 has eaten ONLY long-life (UHT) milk 4-6 x 200 mL per day and plain biscuits; no fruit or vegetables for 3 years

images.shows: Osteopenia, ground-glass metaphyses, thin cortices, Frankel white lines (missed at first reading)

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Scurvy (severe vitamin C deficiency) from extreme selective eating, with iron and vitamin D deficiency
mustDetect: Limp + bleeding gums + petechiae = ask what the child eats
Neurodevelopmental difference + growth failure = risk of restrictive diet
Vitamin C level before more invasive tests
answerKey.pitfall: A jaw biopsy and a bone marrow aspirate were done before anyone asked about diet. Tests whether the engine asks the one question that solves it.
answerKey.outcome: IV vitamin C; walking within 48 hours; full clinical and biochemical resolution by 3 months.

input.patientNarrative: I woke up this morning and my legs were heavy and cramping - I can't walk. They feel numb. This has happened about a dozen times this year, always early morning, and usually goes after an hour or two. Once it happened after drinking at a family party. I ran out of some of my tablets three days ago.
input.clinicianNote: 30M, Samoan. PMH: peptic ulcer disease, hypertension, alcohol and cocaine use disorder; family history of Graves' disease. Meds: methimazole, propranolol, oral potassium (methimazole missed for 3 days). ~10 months ago admitted with leg weakness and K 2.1 - attributed to diarrhoea and lumbar spondylosis. ~6 months ago admitted with profound hypokalaemia, weakness and shallow breathing, had a cardiac arrest. Today: vitals within normal ranges; profound bilateral lower-limb weakness; cranial nerves intact.

vitals.notes: Within normal physiological ranges (values not reported); ECG shows sinus tachycardia

labs.name: ECG
labs.value: sinus tachycardia; inverted U waves in lead II

images.shows: Inverted U waves in lead II

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Recurrent thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (Graves' disease), triggered by missed methimazole and alcohol
keyDifferentials: Lumbar spine disease (an earlier wrong label)
mustDetect: K 2.0 with ECG changes and a prior hypokalaemic cardiac arrest = cardiac monitoring
Methimazole on the medication list = thyrotoxicosis: link it to the paralysis
Replace potassium cautiously (rebound hyperkalaemia); non-selective beta-blocker
answerKey.pitfall: Earlier episodes were blamed on diarrhoea and back disease and no one checked the thyroid until he arrested. The answer is in the medication list.
answerKey.outcome: IV potassium and magnesium on telemetry, methimazole and propranolol restarted; weakness resolved; referred for definitive thyroid treatment.

input.patientNarrative: Two days ago I got a bad pain over my right forehead and around my right eye. The next day blisters came up on my forehead, my right upper eyelid and the tip of my nose. My vision is fine.
input.clinicianNote: 40M accountant, immunocompetent, no history, no alcohol. Day 2 of right frontal and periorbital pain; vesicular rash in right V1 distribution including the nasal tip (Hutchinson's sign); no V2 involvement. Visual acuity 1.0 (20/20) both eyes; anterior and posterior segments normal.

labs.name: MRI brain and orbits with contrast
labs.value: right optic nerve enhancement; right frontal pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement

labs.name: CSF
labs.value: 0 WBC, protein 48 mg/dL, glucose 67 mg/dL; culture negative

labs.name: Blood count, ESR, CRP, HIV, hepatitis, AQP4 and MOG antibodies

images.shows: Right optic disc oedema, RNFL 114 um

stages.2: Day 4 (on oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily since day 2): blurred vision right eye, acuity hand movements, right relative afferent pupillary defect, right optic disc swelling. Left eye normal.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (Hutchinson's sign positive) complicated by optic neuritis, later bilateral, in an immunocompetent adult
answerKey.requiredAction: Stage 1: antiviral today AND same-day ophthalmology review because of Hutchinson's sign. Stage 2: emergency admission, IV aciclovir.
mustDetect: Rash on the tip of the nose = nasociliary branch = high risk of eye involvement
New visual loss in HZO = emergency
Monitor the other eye
answerKey.pitfall: Stage 1 looks like routine shingles with normal vision. An engine that says 'GP, oral antivirals, no referral' fails.
answerKey.outcome: Despite IV aciclovir, IV methylprednisolone and IVIG, the right eye went to no light perception; left eye recovered to 0.9.

input.patientNarrative: My legs have gone weak and tingly and I keep falling. I came in 10 days ago after a fall and they scanned my head and neck and sent me home, but it's worse - I can't feel my legs properly and I walk like I'm drunk. I nearly black out when I stand up. I've used a lot of 'hippy crack' balloons recently.
input.clinicianNote: 66M, history of alcohol and inhalant misuse; heavy nitrous oxide use 2 weeks ago. Bilateral leg weakness, paraesthesia, gait ataxia, recurrent ground-level falls. First ED visit: CT head and cervical spine normal - discharged. Now (day 10): loss of vibration sense to mid-thoracic level; legs 3-4/5; finger-nose and heel-shin ataxia; increased tone with hyporeflexia in all limbs.

images.shows: Symmetric dorsal column hyperintensity - 'inverted V' sign

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord from vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia), precipitated by nitrous oxide
keyDifferentials: Traumatic spinal cord injury (the first label)
mustDetect: Nitrous oxide + myelopathy + macrocytosis = B12 deficiency: treat with IM B12 now (do not wait)
Orthostatic drop to 64/48 = falls risk / autonomic involvement
answerKey.pitfall: Anchored on trauma because of the falls. Also a slang test: the patient says 'hippy crack balloons', not 'nitrous oxide'.
answerKey.outcome: IM B12; sensory ataxia and orthostasis persisted; walking 200 ft with a frame after inpatient rehab.

input.patientNarrative: (Family member) He is confused today and has the chills. His legs keep jerking by themselves - they've jerked on and off for months and the doctors said it was his nerve tablet building up because of his kidneys. Recently his antidepressant was partly switched to a new one, bupropion. Today the nurse said his blood pressure is dangerously high.
input.clinicianNote: M late 70s, BMI 23. Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy with HFrEF, CKD (eGFR 25-40), AF, recurrent depression. Meds: venlafaxine IR (37.5-75 mg/day), amiodarone, apixaban, dapagliflozin, dutasteride, eplerenone, gabapentin, tafamidis, torasemide, metoclopramide prn; bupropion 150 mg/day recently added. Previous episodes: spontaneous clonus on escitalopram (2022); rigidity, clonus, anxiety after venlafaxine started (2024); severe tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, hallucinations, akathisia (2024). Today: confusion, worsening clonus, chills, hypertensive crisis.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Serotonin syndrome (recurrent; Hunter criteria) from low-dose venlafaxine with reduced CYP2D6 activity, worsened by bupropion, amiodarone and metoclopramide (CYP2D6 inhibitors)
keyDifferentials: Gabapentin toxicity in CKD (the earlier explanation)
mustDetect: Spontaneous clonus + confusion on a serotonergic drug = serotonin syndrome
Recent addition of a CYP2D6 inhibitor (bupropion) - drug interaction check
Stop serotonergic drugs; metoclopramide is also serotonergic
answerKey.pitfall: The clonus had been attributed to gabapentin accumulation for months. Tests medication-interaction reasoning, not symptom matching.
answerKey.outcome: All antidepressants stopped; tremor and clonus resolved completely; mood improved.

source.citation: Bouti LNA et al. BMJ Case Rep 2026;19(9):e273316

input.patientNarrative: (Parent) Two weeks ago my 9-year-old had flu and a bit of diarrhoea. Four days ago her arms started getting weak and it's getting worse - she can't lift them properly. Her legs are OK. She had Guillain-Barre when she was two, but that started in her legs, so I don't think it's that.
input.clinicianNote: 9F, normal development, vaccinated. Typical ascending GBS at age 2 (IVIG, full recovery). Influenza-like illness with transient diarrhoea 15 days ago. 4 days of symmetric, progressive upper-limb weakness. Conscious, afebrile. Both arms 3/5. No sensory change, no cranial nerve signs, no sphincter disturbance.

labs.name: Serum and stool botulinum toxin; stool polio culture

images.shows: Enhancement of cauda equina nerve roots

stages.2: Within 24 hours: flaccid weakness of all four limbs, difficulty swallowing, loss of cough reflex, shallow breathing, absent reflexes everywhere; estimated vital capacity < 15 mL/kg.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Recurrent Guillain-Barre syndrome with descending (pharyngeal-cervical-brachial pattern) paralysis, anti-GT1a/GQ1b positive, progressing to respiratory failure
mustDetect: Progressive symmetric weakness after infection = GBS even when it starts in the arms; normal early CSF does not exclude it
Check bulbar function and vital capacity; risk of respiratory failure
Stage 2: lost cough reflex + VC < 15 mL/kg = intubate
answerKey.pitfall: The mother rules GBS out herself because it 'started in the arms'. A normal first CSF can falsely reassure.
answerKey.outcome: Intubated, three IVIG courses, tracheostomy, weaned day 50; complete recovery at 3 months.

source.citation: Ed Dafali L et al. Cureus 2026;18(7):e113362

input.patientNarrative: (Family member) She has heart failure, diabetes, blood pressure and COPD. Today she's confused, short of breath, has chest pain behind the breastbone, stomach pain all over, and keeps vomiting. Normally she does everything for herself. She takes all her tablets.
input.clinicianNote: 62F, HTN, HFpEF, T2DM, COPD; independent at baseline; adherent. Confusion, dyspnoea, retrosternal chest pain, diffuse abdominal pain, persistent vomiting. Bibasal crackles, raised JVP, orthopnoea; finger and toe clubbing; no wheeze, no productive cough. Afebrile. Flu swab negative. CT head normal. CTPA: no PE. Treated as acute decompensated heart failure (CPAP, IV furosemide, GTN), admitted to HDU.

labs.name: ABG (on 24% O2)
labs.value: pH 7.31, pO2 7.4 kPa, pCO2 4.2 kPa, HCO3 17.4, lactate 1.5

stages.2: In HDU despite diuresis and CPAP: worsening agitation needing dexmedetomidine, new paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rate (HR 166) despite bisoprolol, temperature 37.6 C. Echo: EF 55-60%. CT abdomen: mesenteric oedema, effusions. Diffuse goitre on neck examination.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky score 80) as the first presentation of Graves' disease, masquerading as decompensated heart failure and delirium
mustDetect: Heart failure + delirium + vomiting + tachyarrhythmia out of proportion = check thyroid function
Amiodarone (iodine) can worsen thyrotoxicosis
Treat with antithyroid drug, steroid, beta-blockade
answerKey.pitfall: Every finding had a plausible cardiac explanation. Thyroid tests were sent only because she failed to improve.
answerKey.outcome: Carbimazole and hydrocortisone; sinus rhythm restored, cognition back to baseline; discharged day 14.

input.patientNarrative: (Mother) A month ago he was seen here for vomiting and they said it was from smoking weed. He's still vomiting, he's lost 25-30 pounds, and for a few days he's had headaches and dizziness. He talks slowly now and sometimes just stares and doesn't answer. He's not himself.
input.clinicianNote: 15M, no history. Cannabis use for ~3 months, continuing. First ED visit 1 month ago: days of nausea, vomiting, headache; UDS THC; labelled cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome. GP 3 weeks later: AST 111, ALT 506, Na 130; CT head 'haemoconcentration only'. Now: ongoing vomiting, 25-30 lb weight loss, headache, dizziness. On admission: slowed speech, mild confusion, brief episodes of unresponsiveness to voice. CT abdomen: non-specific gastroenteritis.

stages.2: Day 3-4 of admission: sodium corrected to 133 but no cognitive improvement; still bed-bound; new blurred vision, horizontal nystagmus with photophobia, truncal ataxia and mild right dysmetria when he tries to walk.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency) from prolonged vomiting due to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome
mustDetect: Weeks of vomiting + weight loss + confusion = give IV thiamine now, before glucose; do not wait for the level
Wernicke does not need alcohol, and a normal MRI does not exclude it
Stage 2 has the full triad (confusion, eye signs, ataxia)
answerKey.pitfall: Anchored on hyponatraemia and cannabis. In stage 1 only confusion is present - the triad is incomplete in most real cases.
answerKey.outcome: IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily; nystagmus and cognition improved within a day, walking unaided by day 6; full recovery after stopping cannabis.

input.patientNarrative: (Family member) Three days ago she got an itchy rash all over. An allergy tablet helped, then two days ago it came back worse. The clinic said hives and gave her a steroid injection. This afternoon her chest went tight, she couldn't breathe and was sweating cold, and she coughed up pink froth. The local hospital put a breathing tube in. She has never been ill before.
input.clinicianNote: 38F, previously well, no hypertension or diabetes. 3/7 generalized rash, partly better with ebastine; recurred and became confluent 2/7 ago -> 'acute urticaria' -> single IV methylprednisolone 80 mg + ebastine. 8 h ago sudden chest tightness, dyspnoea, cold sweats. At referring hospital: BP 147/106, HR 160, SpO2 60%, pink frothy sputum -> intubated. Now ventilated in our ED.

vitals.notes: Intubated and ventilated. At referring hospital: BP 147/106, HR 160, SpO2 60%

labs.name: Bedside echo
labs.value: nearly absent LV systolic function; dilated LA and LV

stages.2: VF arrest, defibrillated; VA-ECMO started. Coronaries normal. Treated as fulminant viral myocarditis with methylprednisolone 80 mg IV every 8 h and IVIG; troponin keeps rising and VF recurs.
stages.3: Thyroid function normal, cortisol normal. CT abdomen on day 7 shows a left adrenal mass.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Phaeochromocytoma crisis (catecholamine cardiomyopathy, cardiogenic shock, VT/VF) triggered by IV methylprednisolone
mustDetect: Young woman, sudden shock with flash pulmonary oedema, early hypertension, hypokalaemia and glucose 32 shortly after a steroid = catecholamine excess
Steroids can trigger phaeochromocytoma crisis - stop them
Needs alpha-blockade before beta-blockade
answerKey.pitfall: More steroids were given for presumed myocarditis, which likely made it worse. Tests whether the engine connects the drug timeline to the crash.
answerKey.outcome: Alpha then beta blockade on ECMO; laparoscopic adrenalectomy; full LV recovery, normotensive at 1 year.

source.citation: Hu Z et al. Front Med 2026;13:1779740

input.patientNarrative: I started vomiting after eating takeaway food. I have a fever, I'm sweating a lot and my whole body aches. No rash, no headache, no stiff neck, no problem with light, no stomach pain. I'm normally healthy.
input.clinicianNote: 22M, previously well. Acute vomiting after eating outside food; fever, profuse sweating, generalized myalgia. Denies rash, headache, photophobia, abdominal pain, neurological symptoms. Febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic; BP improved transiently with IV fluid. No rash or meningism documented.

labs.name: Blood culture
labs.value: Gram-negative diplococci at 10 h; Neisseria meningitidis serogroup W135

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Fulminant meningococcaemia (N. meningitidis W135) with septic shock and DIC, presenting as gastroenteritis without rash or meningism
keyDifferentials: Septic shock from bacterial gastroenteritis (the admitting diagnosis)
Severe malaria / dengue in a traveller
mustDetect: Shock + leukopenia + DIC (PT 120 s, fibrinogen 60) in a healthy young adult = fulminant sepsis: antibiotics within the hour
Absence of rash does not exclude meningococcus
Close-contact prophylaxis and public health notification
answerKey.pitfall: The food story anchors to gastroenteritis, and the patient's long list of denials (no rash, no headache, no stiff neck) is a negation test - the labs show he is dying.
answerKey.outcome: Ceftriaxone started; sudden agitation, collapse and cardiac arrest; did not survive. (The paper's second patient, 31M with an acute abdomen, survived.)

input.patientNarrative: My muscles ache all over and I'm suddenly short of breath. No fever, no cough, no chest pain. I had breast cancer this year - operation and chemo, and I've just started the targeted treatment.
input.clinicianNote: 50F. Generalized myalgia and new hypoxaemic respiratory failure; denies fever, cough, chest pain. PMH: ulcerative colitis (topical mesalazine); HER2+ breast cancer this year - right mastectomy and axillary clearance, doxorubicin + cyclophosphamide x4 (stopped), 1 cycle trastuzumab; HTN, dyslipidaemia, ex-smoker. No travel or exposures. Infection and PE excluded in ED. Day 1 on ward: drowsy, psychomotor slowing, no focal deficit; CT brain normal. Ultrasound: hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly.

vitals.notes: Hypoxaemic respiratory failure (values not reported); afebrile by history

labs.name: Blood/urine cultures, CSF, HIV, hepatitis, CMV, EBV (past), HSV, parvovirus, Rickettsia conorii

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HScore 211 -> 246), probably chemotherapy-triggered
keyDifferentials: Metastatic breast cancer with marrow infiltration
mustDetect: Ferritin > 10,000 + cytopenias + high triglycerides + hepatomegaly + encephalopathy = HLH: calculate HScore
Haematology referral and dexamethasone without delay
answerKey.pitfall: No fever (HLH usually has fever) and an obvious alternative (cancer on chemotherapy). Tests whether the engine recognises the ferritin pattern.
answerKey.outcome: Dexamethasone (HLH-94); full haematological recovery; resumed cancer therapy; no relapse at 4 years.

input.patientNarrative: For six hours I've had crushing pain in the middle of my chest and I'm pouring with sweat. I've also got a headache and feel dizzy. My eyesight is fine, no nausea, no stomach pain. I had some drinks at a work party about a day and a bit ago.
input.clinicianNote: 45M, previously healthy. 6 h crushing substernal chest pain, profuse diaphoresis, headache, dizziness. Denies visual disturbance, nausea, abdominal pain. Alcohol at a social gathering ~30 h ago (type and amount not disclosed). Diaphoretic, distressed. Pupils 3 mm, equal and reactive; neurologically normal. Triple rule-out CT angiogram: no coronary occlusion, dissection or PE. Echo: lateral wall hypokinesis. No blood gas has been taken.

labs.name: ECG
labs.value: sinus tachycardia; ST depression 0.05-0.10 mV V4-V6; T-wave flattening

labs.name: ABG
labs.value: pH 7.08, HCO3 8.5, base excess -18.5, anion gap 34, lactate 5.8

images.shows: Subarachnoid blood; later massive right basal ganglia haemorrhage with necrosis

stages.2: 3 hours later (after aspirin 300 mg, clopidogrel 300 mg and enoxaparin for presumed NSTEMI): suddenly unresponsive, pupils unequal (L 4 mm, R 5 mm). Two co-workers from the same party arrive with blurred vision.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Methanol poisoning (adulterated alcohol) mimicking acute coronary syndrome, complicated by haemorrhagic basal ganglia necrosis made worse by dual antiplatelet therapy and heparin
mustDetect: Alcohol ~30 h ago + unexplained illness = ask for blood gas, anion gap and osmolar gap BEFORE antiplatelets/anticoagulants
Clusters of sick people from one gathering = toxic exposure
Fomepizole or ethanol, bicarbonate, dialysis
answerKey.pitfall: Every finding fits a heart attack, and the patient denies the classic visual symptoms. A blood gas was never sent until he collapsed.
answerKey.outcome: Bicarbonate, ethanol, dialysis, folate, craniotomy (2.5 L blood loss); died of multi-organ failure at 2 weeks.

source.citation: Zhu J et al. Front Cardiovasc Med 2026;13:1801376

input.patientNarrative: For a month I've had fevers up to 39 and my muscles ache all over. It came on slowly. My stomach is fine - no pain, no diarrhoea, I haven't lost weight. I haven't travelled, nobody around me is sick, and I'm not on any new medicines.
input.clinicianNote: 33F, no history. 1 month gradual-onset myalgia with documented fever to 39 C. No GI symptoms, no weight loss reported, no travel, contacts or new drugs. Pale, thin, not distressed. No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no focal neurology. Tachycardic and hypotensive -> admitted.

labs.name: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
labs.value: no malignancy, abscess or vascular disease

labs.name: Duodenal biopsy
labs.value: partial villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh IIIa)

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Coeliac disease presenting as fever of unknown origin with iron-deficiency anaemia
mustDetect: Vital signs (HR 130, BP 95/55) need same-day assessment even though the eventual cause is chronic
Iron deficiency (ferritin 7) in a thin young woman with no blood loss = test for coeliac disease
Prolonged fever with negative infection, cancer and autoimmune work-up -> widen the differential
answerKey.pitfall: No gut symptoms at all. Tests whether the engine links unexplained iron deficiency to malabsorption, and whether it still triages on the abnormal vitals.
answerKey.outcome: IV iron and gluten-free diet; CRP normal by day 10; well with weight gain at 3 months.

source.citation: Abdouh S et al. Oxf Med Case Reports 2026;2026(10):omag180

input.patientNarrative: (Paramedic handover) 35-year-old, 26 weeks pregnant with her fifth baby; she had pre-eclampsia in two earlier pregnancies. Two hours of severe headache 9/10, pain under the ribs in the middle and blurred vision - she thought it was a cold and took paracetamol. She then had a fit in her sleep at home and a second fit on the bus on the way here.
input.clinicianNote: 35F G5P4 at 26+1 weeks. Previous pre-eclampsia x2 (at 39 and 20 weeks). Severe headache, epigastric pain, blurred vision, photophobia. Two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Now conscious and oriented, post-ictal: dysarthria, tongue bite, urinary incontinence. No respiratory distress, haemodynamically stable. Vital signs within normal range - no hypertension recorded. Fundal height appropriate, single live cephalic fetus, FHR 138, no contractions. No history of epilepsy. Lives in Quito, Ecuador.

vitals.notes: Within normal range including blood pressure (values not reported)

labs.name: CT brain (non-contrast)
labs.value: multiple intra-axial cystic and calcified lesions, no mass effect or hydrocephalus

labs.name: MRI brain
labs.value: multiple parenchymal cysts with visible scolices (vesicular and colloidal stages), perilesional oedema

stages.2: Magnesium sulfate started for eclampsia. Seizures recur and neurological symptoms persist despite magnesium; blood pressure still normal.

answerKey.finalDiagnosis: Neurocysticercosis (multiple vesicular/colloidal parenchymal cysts) causing seizures in pregnancy, mimicking eclampsia
mustDetect: Stage 1: seizures in pregnancy after 20 weeks = treat as eclampsia (magnesium) - this is correct and safe
Stage 2: normotensive + seizures recurring despite magnesium = neuroimaging now
In endemic areas (Latin America, Eastern Cape, much of sub-Saharan Africa) neurocysticercosis is a leading cause of adult-onset seizures
answerKey.pitfall: The engine should NOT drop eclampsia at stage 1. The test is whether, at stage 2, it widens the differential instead of escalating magnesium alone.
answerKey.outcome: Levetiracetam controlled seizures; vaginal delivery of a healthy baby at 37+3 weeks; albendazole and steroids after delivery; seizure-free.

source.citation: Ochoa-Andrade M et al. Front Med 2026;13:1900625
